items.title: Read spatial and time wave records
items.student: Supplied transverse-wave profile at one instant:crests at x0.20,1.00,1.80m with displacement+0.030m;trough displacement−0.030m;equilibrium0. A fixed point has successive crests at t0,0.25,0.50s. Draw a labelled spatial profile and a separate displacement-time sketch. Find amplitude,peak-to-peak displacement,wavelength,period and frequency. Explain why a spatial crest separation and a time between crests have different units. Contrast transverse displacement with longitudinal sound compressions in air.
items.teacher: Amplitude0.030m,peak-to-peak0.060m,λ0.80m,T0.25s,f4Hz. Space graph xaxisdistance;time graph xaxistime. Sound in air is longitudinal particle oscillation parallel to propagation;transverse profile is a representation of a different oscillation direction,not literal up/down sound particles. Wave transport transfers energy,not every particle travelling with the wave.

items.title: Interpret v=fλ rather than recite it
items.student: A periodic wave advances one wavelength during one period. Explain v=λ/T=fλ using distance/time and f=1/T. For a model with v12m/s,f3Hz,findλ andT. If frequency becomes6Hz while speed in the same nondispersive model stays12m/s,find newλ/T. Explain why doubling frequency need not double speed and why amplitude is absent from this linear relation.
items.teacher: Initialλ4m,T1/3≈0.333s;newλ2m,T1/6≈0.167s. Fixedmedium/model speed gives inverse frequency-wavelength relation. Amplitude not in this linear wave-speed equation;do not generalise to all nonlinear/dispersive contexts. Symbol v is propagation speed here,not particle oscillation velocity.

items.title: Wave-equation calculations and units
items.student: For supplied models calculate:A speed fromf50Hz,λ0.40m;Bfrequencyfromv340m/s,λ0.85m;C wavelengthfromv300m/s,f1.5kHz;Dperiodfromf25Hz. Convert kHz toHz andshowunits/rearrangement. Explain why using1.5 directly in C gives a thousand-fold error. None is an actual measured wave.
items.teacher: A20m/s;B400Hz;C1500Hz→0.20m;D0.040s. Checkv=fλ andT=1/f dimensionally. Speed/wavelength values are task-specific conditions,not universal for all sound. Do not identify an unknown medium from these numbers alone.

items.title: A boundary can change speed and wavelength
items.student: Supplied periodic source frequency5Hz;wave speed20m/s in mediumA and10m/s in mediumB. Assuming stationary boundary and unchanged source frequency,calculate wavelengths and periods in both. Draw schematic equally timed wavefronts with closer spacing inB. Explain which properties change and why frequency stays fixed. Refraction means direction changes when entering obliquely under suitable speed change;normal incidence can change speed/λ without bending.
items.teacher: λA4m,λB2m,T0.20s both,f5Hz both. Frequency remains source-driven in this stationary model. Do not preserveλ while changingv at fixedf. Slower medium bends an oblique ray towardnormal;not every boundary requires bending atnormalincidence. No specific real medium or measurement inferred.

items.title: Reflection with a defined normal
items.student: Draw a flat reflecting surface and a normal at the incident point. A ray makes35° with the normal;draw and label the reflected ray and both angles. Compare reflection of light in a mirror with sound echo at a wall. Explain that incident/reflected angles are measured from the normal,not surface,and ideal reflection stays in the original medium. No laser or mirror-glare experiment.
items.teacher: Reflection angle35° from normal,55° from surface;incident/reflected rays opposite sides ofnormal in sameplane. Reflection changes propagation direction,not necessarily sourcefrequency. Mirrors/light and walls/sound share a model but materials/absorption/scattering differ. A diagram is not an actual demonstration.

items.title: Echo method with an actual-action boundary
items.student: Conditional actual observation:teacher selects a quiet,approved level area away from roads/traffic/hearing-sensitive activity,with a suitable distant reflecting wall and safe standing zone. Use one moderate hand clap,not amplified sound,shouting,impulses near ears or repeated noise escalation. Record whether a distinct delayed echo is heard;an absent/unclear echo is a valid observation,not permission to get louder. Assign actual source/listener/recorder roles and record site/date/conditions. If no approved suitable site,use supplied records and mark not performed. Supplied fictional echo round-trip time0.40s with sound speed340m/s:find wall distance. Compare a second record wall17m away:find round-trip time. Explain why reverberation in a small room may not be a separately resolved echo and why ordinary reaction timing cannot precisely measure such short delays. No actual speed/distance is prefilled.
items.teacher: d340×0.40/2=68m;for17m,t2×17/340=0.10s. Out-and-back path gives factor2. Actual quiet-site approval/roles/heard-or-not record needed for demonstration;paper values are not fieldmeasurements. Multiple close reflections can blur into reverberation;no precisionclaim fromhumanreactiontiming. Stopratherthanraiselevel if conditionsunsuitable.

items.title: Sound refraction:day/night is a conditional model
items.student: Supplied temperature-only profiles,ignoring wind:CaseD ground air warmer than air above;CaseN ground air cooler with warmer layer above. Sound speed is greater in warmer air. Draw two height diagrams with speed-gradient labels and initially near-horizontal sound rays:predict bending for each and explain why sound may reach different ground locations. Qualify the common day/night association:neither clocktime alone nor one listening report establishes the gradient,wind,humidity or audibility. Reference:Penn State Acoustics,https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/demos/refract/refract.html. Optional approved video needs teacher-provided title/link and actual viewing record;these diagrams are not a watched clip.
items.teacher: D speed decreases withheight,rays curveupward towardslower region;N speed increaseswithheight,rays curvebackdown towardcooler/slowerground. Suchprofilesmay occuronsunnydays/clearnights,butnotalways. Windgradients,source/receiverheight,terrain/backgroundnoise andotherconditionsmatter. No universal'nightsoundalwaysfarther'laws or localweatherevidence. These are gradient rays,not abrupt surface-reflection bounces.

items.title: Diffraction depends on relative scale
items.student: Supplied barrier openings:gap0.50m. SoundAλ0.85m,soundBλ0.085m;compare wavelength/gap ratios and predict which tends to spread more strongly in this simplified model. Draw wavefront sketches showing spreading at an opening. Distinguish diffraction aroundedges from reflection offsurfaces and refraction due tospeedvariation. Explain why a light beam with wavelength far smaller than a doorway usually shows muchless obvious doorway spreading than ordinary sound.
items.teacher: Ratios1.7 and0.17;A generallystrongerspreadingwhenwavelengthcomparabletoopening. Diffractionisnot reservedfor gaps exactlyequalλ,andallwavescanshowitunderappropriateconditions. Morewavelengthrelativetogap oftenmoreobviousbending;exactpatternrequiresgeometry. Distinguish fromsurfacebounce andspeed-gradientrefraction.

items.title: Around-corner sound investigation
items.student: Conditional approved observation:in a quiet supervised school area,a speaker uses an ordinary low conversational voice and a listener stands safely around an approved corner/out of direct view;do not obstruct corridors,enter traffic,shout,use earphones or raise volume. Record positions,heard/notheard,backgroundconditions and actualroles/date. Repeat after a small safe position change only if teacher permits. If unsuitable,use this supplied fictional record:'voice audible out of view near a doorway;hard walls present'. Explain why diffraction may contribute,but reflection/transmission andgeometry prevent claiming this single observation proves diffraction alone. Draw a possible diffraction path and a reflected alternative. Mark actual experiment not performed if only suppliedrecordused.
items.teacher: Soundcan diffractaroundedges,andwalls mayalsoreflect;hearingalonecannotisolateone mechanism. Needcontrolledgeometry/sourcelevels andappropriateanalysisforstrongerclaim;avoidprecision/loudnesscomparisonswithoutmeasurement. Actualsafeobservationcan demonstratean effect withlimits,notproveauniquecause. Sourceactualactionrequiresobservedroles/provision;printcarddoesnotcertifyit.

items.title: Environmental wave cases and source distinctions
items.student: Supplied qualitative cases:coastal water waves can move sediment and erode or reshape shorelines,affecting habitats,communities andinfrastructure;water-wave energy can disrupt some port operations. Underwater anthropogenic sound from ships/construction can affect marineanimal communication/behaviour dependingonlevel,frequency,duration andspecies. Identify which case concerns water-surface waves versus acoustic waves;explain possiblebenefits/harms andtwo missing localassessmentfacts. No fieldvisit,shorelineactivity or measuredimpact claimed. References:NOAA OceanService,https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/wavesinocean.html;NOAA Fisheries OceanNoise,https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/national/science-data/ocean-noise.
items.teacher: Do not treatallwavesasone physicalphenomenon orallimpactsasharmful. Coastalsediment/habitatmovement can be natural;effectdependslocalconditions. Underwatersound differsfromwater-surfacewave motion;notallshipsoundcausesinjury. Needsite,exposure,species/habitat,weather/geometry andbaselineevidence;suppliedsummariesarenotlocalmeasurements.

items.title: Mitigation needs evidence and trade-offs
items.student: Fictional coastalcommunity compares A restricting access to an alreadyidentified unsafe shore duringofficialwarnings;B installing an engineeredbreakwater without a study;C reducing avoidableshippingnoise through qualified operationalplanning. Match actions to thewater-wave/acousticcases. Explain why B needs engineering/ecologicalassessment andwhy C'sbenefit cannotbequantifiedfromageneralsummary. Propose an evidence request covering communities,marineecosystems,infrastructure andoperations. No construction,marinevisit or individual emergencyplan isperformed.
items.teacher: A addressespeople'sexposuretoidentifiedwater-wavehazards,subjecttoofficiallocalguidance;B needsqualifieddesign,sediment/habitat/navigationtradeoffs,notautomaticbestsolution;C targetssomeanthropogenicacousticexposure withoperational/ecologicalconstraints. Askforlocalrisk/exposure/habitat/infrastructure/portoperationdata andcommunityinput. No invented percentages,engineeringcertification or universalmitigationverdict.

items.title: Waves and safer road-use reasoning
items.student: Supplied use cards:rear-viewmirror changes lightdirection byreflection;optical lenses change lightpaths byrefraction;horn/siren sound can spread aroundedges bydiffraction andcanalsoreflect. Explain one useandone limitationforeach. Correct thefictionalclaim:'hearingaroundacornerprovestheroadclear,andanymirrorremovesallblindspots'. Draw one reflection/refraction/diffraction model andidentifyactualevidence needed before a real safetydecision. No roadvisit,vehicleoperation,laser or loudsound. Statehowwaveknowledgehelpswhilequalifiedroadproceduresandattentionremainneeded.
items.teacher: Mirrorreflection aidsviewbutgeometry/blindspotsmatter;lensrefraction supportsfocusbutdoesnotcertifyeveryproduct/view;diffractioncanallowhiddenaudiblesources butdirection/distance/absencecannotguaranteeroadclear. Model drawingsnotrealtrafficdetectors. Road-safetydiscussionisconceptual,no legaldrivingrule/safetycertification oractualfielddemonstration inferred.
